questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the United States paid for European recovery
questions.learningObjective: identify the economic self-interest behind the Marshall Plan
questions.stem: In 1947 a US official told Congress that European heavy industry was producing a fraction of its pre-war output and that restoring it was a matter of life or death for the world economy. What did the announcement of the Marshall Plan chiefly serve?

options.text: American industry needed the European market restored, so aid abroad doubled as a plan for work at home

options.misconception: assumes pure generosity toward Europe and ignores the domestic economy entirely
options.text: Europe was rescued from generosity alone, with no interest in American industry shown in it

options.misconception: recasts a market-recovery programme as a plan to govern western Europe directly
options.text: The United States moved to rule western Europe itself rather than let Europeans rebuild

options.misconception: swaps an economic recovery programme for a project to occupy the eastern states
options.text: The plan was designed chiefly to drive Soviet forces out of eastern Europe by military force

questions.explanation: The official's figure is the evidence: output below the pre-war level meant unsold American plant, and rebuilding European heavy industry was the one route back to full employment at home, so generosity and self-interest pointed the same way. The tempting answers each delete that link, treating the programme as pure charity, as a scheme for direct rule, or as a military project in the east, none of which the announcement proposed.
questions.hint: Ask what American factories would have to sell into once Europe was producing again.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Aid conditionality and the coordinating council
questions.learningObjective: explain why aid was tied to jointly drafted plans
questions.stem: An original summary of a 1948 recovery circular tells each invited government to draft a regional programme first, to consult its neighbours before submitting it, and to accept that money would follow the plan rather than replace the need for one. What principle is that circular imposing?

options.text: Aid would pay for coordinated plans, so states would rebuild in harness rather than separately

options.misconception: reads a requirement about economic interdependence as administrative tidiness
options.text: The circular settles only procedure, since the substance of recovery was left to each recipient

options.misconception: mistakes American control of the money for American authorship of every plan
options.text: A single official in Washington wrote each plan, so no European government chose its own projects

options.misconception: turns an economic condition into a military-membership clause the circular lacks
options.text: Recovery funds were withheld from any state that did not join the western military bloc first

questions.explanation: Draft regionally, consult neighbours, and money follows the plan: the circular makes aid a payment for coordination, and an economy rebuilt in harness with its neighbours is one that a state cannot be pried out of the group by a political offer. The tempting answers reduce the condition to neat procedure, hand the writing of the plans to Washington, or invent a military-membership clause the circular nowhere contains.
questions.hint: The word regional and the instruction to consult neighbours are doing the work.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Moscow turns down the aid offer
questions.learningObjective: explain why the eastern states rejected recovery aid
questions.stem: In 1947 the Soviet foreign minister instructed the governments of eastern Europe to refuse the American aid offer, and no eastern government applied for it. What best explains that refusal?

options.text: Stalin read the offer as a device to pry one state out, so unity of the camp came before the money

options.misconception: assumes the eastern economies rebuilt faster, which the reported output figures contradict
options.text: Eastern governments refused because they had already rebuilt further than the western states had

options.misconception: reduces a political refusal to a shipping problem no record of the offer mentions
options.text: The refusal came down to tonnage, since American ships could not reach the eastern ports in time

options.misconception: invents a customs condition that belonged to a later trade agreement, not to this offer
options.text: Aid was refused because the eastern states insisted on keeping every tariff under national control

questions.explanation: An offer that must be planned and negotiated with neighbours is also a channel for influence, and a bloc leader who expects one government to take a first step understands where that leads, so the instruction protects the camp rather than the budget. The tempting answers say the east had already succeeded, blame cargo tonnage, or supply a tariff condition that belonged to a later trade agreement.
questions.hint: Think about who benefits first if a neighbouring government sets the terms.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The blockade of Berlin
questions.learningObjective: identify the trigger and the stake behind the Berlin blockade
questions.stem: In June 1948 the authorities of the western occupation zones issued new banknotes for their own zone, and the Soviet authorities replied by sealing the roads, railways, and canals that served the western sectors of Berlin. What was the response chiefly defending?

options.text: Control of currency and of how the western sectors would be governed within a divided city

options.misconception: invents a western claim to hold eastern elections that the west never asserted
options.text: The right of the western zones to hold elections that would soon cover the whole of the city

options.misconception: confuses a currency measure with the reparations settlement of the preceding decade
options.text: A sovereign claim to reparations for the destruction left in the western part of the city

options.misconception: mistakes a reaction against the west for a proposed reform of the eastern zone
options.text: An eastern plan to bring the western zones into the political programme of the eastern government

questions.explanation: New notes in the western zones meant an economy and an authority running parallel to the eastern one inside a single city, and whoever controls the currency there controls who employs the population, so the sealing defended the eastern monopoly of rule. The tempting answers invent a western election claim, revive a reparations dispute, or read the blockade as a proposal to reform the eastern zone rather than a defence of it.
questions.hint: Ask who employs and pays the people living in a sector when two note systems exist.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: American output and idle capacity, 1940-1950
questions.learningObjective: read a data series for the American economic stake in aid
questions.stem: An American business annual prints pre-war output, a marked fall by 1946, a jump in the share of plants standing idle, and a rebound from 1947 that runs above the pre-war trend. How does that series bear on the American case for rebuilding Europe?

options.text: Idle capacity at home points outward, so foreign demand was the road back to fuller employment

options.misconception: reads idle plants as proof of foreign self-sufficiency, which reverses the series
options.text: The rebound shows Europe needed nothing, so American exports mattered only in the bad year

options.misconception: denies the very economic stake that the idle-plant figure is evidence for
options.text: The idle plants show the United States had no economic reason at all to aid Europe

options.misconception: moves the recovery to a year the series places before the fall, not after it
options.text: The rebound proves the problem was solved at home by 1945, before any aid was discussed

questions.explanation: Idle plants are capacity that exists and earns nothing, and the only way to work that capacity is to find a buyer, so a government watching the share of idle plants rise had a direct interest in the demand that rebuilding Europe would create; the later rebound shows the line the programme is meant to restore. The tempting answers use the same series to claim Europe was self-sufficient, deny the stake outright, or place the recovery before the fall the table actually prints.
questions.hint: Idle plants are a cost to whoever owns them, so ask who else gains from working them.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a collective guarantee is for
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the political function of a mutual defence treaty
questions.stem: A foreign secretary argues that a lone promise to send armies across the sea will be broken the first time it is tested, while a treaty signed by a dozen governments will not be. What is the strongest reason his own government is better off inside such an alliance?

options.text: Aid to an attacked member becomes automatic, so no government is left to face an attack by itself

options.misconception: confuses an alliance of states with a body where one member simply commands
options.text: The largest member decides every question by vote, so the smaller partners only follow its lead

options.misconception: assumes the treaty substitutes a purchase of defence for the need for any national force
options.text: National armies become unnecessary, since defence can be bought outright from the strongest member

options.misconception: misreads a guarantee against attack as a schedule for paying a fixed share of costs
options.text: The cost of defence is fixed in advance, so members never have to debate what to contribute

questions.explanation: The secretary's own test is the argument: a pledge by one government is a promise about a future nobody controls, while a signed treaty turns help into an obligation no member can quietly abandon without the alliance, which raises the cost of walking out for every government considering it. The tempting answers replace the guarantee with a command structure, with the abolition of national defence, or with a budget schedule, none of which is what a mutual defence treaty does.
questions.hint: The question is what stops a member abandoning the others at the worst moment.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Rearmament and the end of occupation
questions.learningObjective: explain the bargain behind West German rearmament
questions.stem: In 1954 a West German leader told his parliament that the occupation of the country was ending and full sovereignty was returning, and in the same year his government agreed to raise armed forces of its own. Why accept the force as part of the bargain?

options.text: Sovereignty was incomplete without armed forces, so an army was the price of being an independent state

options.misconception: believes rearmament was demanded to match the eastern army rather than to end the occupation
options.text: The west wanted a second equal army in the east, so the force was built for balance against the other side

options.misconception: asserts a defence-command condition the 1954 agreements did not attach to rearmament
options.text: The force was the entry fee for a European defence command, so the army preceded the alliance

options.misconception: ties a military decision to the currency reform of four years earlier, which it did not concern
options.text: Rearmament undid the currency reform, so the state recovered the monetary control it had lost

questions.explanation: Sovereignty is the ability to act on your own account, and a state forbidden any armed forces of its own remains under a foreign occupier's command in the one sphere where command is tested, so the government paid with the very thing the constitution and the occupier both required. The tempting answers turn rearmament into a balancing measure, an entry fee for a larger command, or a monetary repair, none of which the 1954 settlement concerned.
questions.hint: Ask what a state is still forbidden that every fully sovereign state may do.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: An eastern bloc treaty presented as mutual defence
questions.learningObjective: interpret a treaty summary as public presentation
questions.stem: An original summary of a 1955 eastern bloc treaty records that an armed attack on one member counts as an attack on all, and that the allied forces will be directed by one command. Why was that treaty concluded in the same year a western neighbour joined the rival alliance?

options.text: Control of the bloc had to be shown as mutual defence once a western neighbour joined the other alliance

options.misconception: confuses a military treaty with a monetary arrangement the bloc did not then possess
options.text: The eastern states needed one currency, so a military treaty was the shortest route to a common bank

options.misconception: invents a decisive war the treaty year does not contain, unlike the conflict two years before
options.text: The eastern bloc had just won a war in the west, so the treaty recorded the terms of that victory

options.misconception: assumes the treaty dissolved the earlier agreement, which it explicitly set beside itself
options.text: The eastern states wanted to end the old alliance, so the new treaty replaced everything signed earlier

questions.explanation: Attack on one is attack on all, with one command, is the vocabulary of a collective defence pact, and a bloc whose control of its members rested on troops and a party line needed that vocabulary in the very year the division became visible across the inner border. The tempting answers read the treaty as a monetary scheme, invent a decisive war to explain its date, or claim it dissolved the earlier agreement it in fact supplemented.
questions.hint: The language of a defence pact is a public claim about who is defending whom.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Britain's exit from Greece and the containment policy
questions.learningObjective: explain why a British withdrawal changed the containment policy
questions.stem: In 1947 the British government, unable to keep paying for a campaign against an armed insurgency, told Washington it was leaving. Explain why that departure mattered more than a change of government in the capital.

options.text: The withdrawal left a gap, so aid came to keep a government in place and containment became a policy here

options.misconception: claims a complete insurgent victory that the campaign's record plainly contradicts
options.text: Governments turned over constantly, since the insurgents had already won the fighting in the mountains

options.misconception: reduces a change of policy to a change in warships, ignoring the money that drove it
options.text: The departure mattered only for the fleet, since the navy alone decided who governed the country

options.misconception: claims a domestic spending effect and drops the strategic question entirely
options.text: It mattered for the treasury alone, since the money saved was spent on roads in the north

questions.explanation: A state that cannot fund a campaign stops funding it, and a power withdrawing from a country with an armed insurgency leaves a vacuum that a third party fills under a stated doctrine, which is exactly what turned containment from a claim about distant Asia into a European commitment. The tempting answers credit the insurgents with total victory, reduce the change to warships, or report only a budget effect and abandon the strategic question.
questions.hint: Ask what a third party does with a position that a tired ally has just given up.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: An Asian state enters the western alliance
questions.learningObjective: recall the strategic reason a state outside Europe joined the defence system
questions.stem: A state on the western edge of Asia was admitted to the western alliance in 1952. What was the chief strategic reason for drawing a country that lies largely outside Europe into a European defence system?

options.text: Its position commands the sea passage into the Black Sea and it shares a long border with the USSR

options.misconception: invents an industrial dependence the alliance never used as a reason for membership
options.text: Its heavy industry had grown so large that European defence now depended on its steel and coal

options.misconception: assumes a shared currency came first, whereas the common money arrived decades later
options.text: Its government had adopted a shared currency, so the alliance admitted it to defend that money

options.misconception: attributes the admission to resources in a region the state never controlled
options.text: Its territory held the largest oil fields in the region, which the alliance needed to place under guard

questions.explanation: Alliances are drawn where a power can be reached, and a state that commands the sea approach to the Black Sea and shares a frontier with the Soviet Union is a position that can be closed against it, which is a fact about defence rather than about industry or money. The tempting answers substitute heavy industry, a shared currency adopted decades later, and oil fields the state never held.
questions.hint: Ask what an opponent would have to do to reach the other members through this country.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A state kept outside the western defence system
questions.learningObjective: recall why one regime stayed outside the post-war settlements
questions.stem: An original summary of a 1953 parliamentary debate records an argument that a government which crushed its opponents at the end of a civil war cannot join a defence alliance, because membership would let those opponents return. What does that argument help to explain?

options.text: The country stayed outside the alliance and its economic programmes for decades after the war

options.misconception: predicts the opposite of what happened, since the country was not admitted in the 1950s
options.text: The country joined the alliance at once and became its largest single member before 1956

options.misconception: invents a command arrangement that the debate summary nowhere describes
options.text: Its armed forces were placed under a foreign command in exchange for admission in the 1950s

options.misconception: invents an aid entitlement that the exclusion in fact denied the country
options.text: Its economy received the largest single share of the recovery aid offered in the late 1940s

questions.explanation: Membership would restore the opponents the regime had destroyed, so the government had every reason to price the alliance as a threat and to prefer the economic isolation that came with it, which is why the country stayed outside the military and financial arrangements for years. The tempting answers claim prompt admission, an imposed foreign command, or a large share of recovery aid, none of which followed from the exclusion the debate is defending.
questions.hint: Ask what a government built on crushing its opponents would lose by joining a body of states.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The break between Moscow and one eastern government
questions.learningObjective: explain the cause of the split inside the eastern bloc
questions.stem: In 1948 one eastern government was thrown out of the party bureau that coordinated the bloc, and its leader answered that the quarrel was over the pace of change inside his own country. What was really being contested behind that charge?

options.text: Stalin would not accept a government deciding its own pace, since a precedent there ends his control

options.misconception: invents a currency dispute the bloc did not have, since it issued no common money
options.text: Stalin demanded a common currency, and the state refused to price its goods in eastern accounts

options.misconception: replaces a party dispute with a separate defence agreement that no source records
options.text: The state had signed its own defence agreement, and the bureau resented the guarantee behind it

options.misconception: reduces a substantive split to a change of name with no institutional content
options.text: The state had only just become a communist one, so the bureau objected to the title alone

questions.explanation: A bloc held together by a single party and a single command cannot survive a member legislating its own path, because the first state permitted to decide how fast it changes becomes a precedent, and the leader of the bloc must either accept the precedent or cut the state out. The tempting answers invent a currency quarrel, a secret defence arrangement, and a dispute about the state's name, none of which caused the split.
questions.hint: Ask what Moscow loses if one member is allowed to set its own pace.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ireland leaves the Commonwealth
questions.learningObjective: recall the interest calculation behind a peaceful decolonization
questions.stem: A dominion on which the crown had spent little, whose army had not fought in the war, and which declared itself a republic in 1949, was left without a fight. Why did the other dominions accept it?

options.text: It was the one dominion serving no British interest, so holding it by force was not worth the cost

options.misconception: treats a declaration as a legal novelty when dominion status had been traded away
options.text: It was already legally independent, so the declaration only announced a fact settled in law

options.misconception: moves the declaration back to the war, when the state was still a dominion
options.text: It had been a republic since the war began, so no institution and no allegiance actually changed

options.misconception: assumes a trading reason for release that the calculation of strategic value denies
options.text: Its economy was growing so fast that Britain preferred to reach the market from outside the empire

questions.explanation: Empire is kept while it pays, and this dominion furnished neither a strategic position nor a market worth a garrison, so the cost of holding it outweighed the return and a republic cost nothing to concede. The tempting answers claim the release was already legal, push the declaration back before the war, or invent a commercial reason for letting go that the interest calculation contradicts.
questions.hint: Ask what the empire was getting back from this particular possession each year.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Transfer of power in India, 1947
questions.learningObjective: explain why Britain handed over power within months
questions.stem: Britain announced in 1947 that it would transfer power in India within months, at a moment when the country faced famine, partition, and communal killing. Explain why the government moved so quickly.

options.text: The claim behind empire had already been broken, so holding India by force would cost more than it gave

options.misconception: reads a retreat from an untenable position as a reward for loyal service
options.text: The transfer rewarded loyal service, so the government chose to recognise decades of service

options.misconception: compresses years of negotiation and pressure into a single week's decision
options.text: A single commission report forced the decision, so the announcement came within one week of it

options.misconception: claims the transfer solved a crisis the same period shows worsening
options.text: The transfer ended the famine, so Britain withdrew once the harvests and the rationing were in order

questions.explanation: A power that has just fought a global war and now faces a mass political movement cannot simply reconquer a subcontinent, and once the claim to rule by consent was denied in public, spending more to hold it would have defended an idea no one at home would pay for, so speed was a way of leaving without appearing to be chased out. The tempting answers make the transfer a reward, compress it into one commission's report, and claim it solved the famine that same period shows worsening.
questions.hint: Ask whether force was cheaper than continuing, and whether the claim to rule still held.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: France fights to keep Indochina
questions.learningObjective: explain why one colony was worth an eight-year war
questions.stem: After the surrender in 1945 France moved to reassert its authority in Indochina, and the war that followed lasted eight years and ended in defeat. Why was that effort worth so much to the French state?

options.text: The colonies carried the army, the flag, and the claim to rank, so losing one damaged all three at once

options.misconception: invents a resource stake the region never held for the French recovery programme
options.text: The territory held the coal and steel the French recovery plan needed, so the economy demanded it back

options.misconception: denies the difficulty of the fighting that an eight-year war plainly records
options.text: The effort was cheap, since the forces opposing France were small and badly armed throughout

options.misconception: moves the effect to Europe, where the campaign spent money rather than gaining anything
options.text: The campaign restored French authority in Europe, since the colonies paid for the armies kept there

questions.explanation: France had been defeated and occupied, and in that condition the overseas territories were the proof that the country was still a great power, so losing Indochina was read as evidence that the empire and the rank it carried were both going, which is why the government paid for eight years of war rather than concede the point. The tempting answers invent a resource requirement, deny how hard the fighting was, and claim a European gain the campaign in fact only drained.
questions.hint: Ask what losing one colony does to a country's claim about its own standing.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A new state in central Africa inherits colonial borders
questions.learningObjective: evaluate which step most reduces the risk of state collapse
questions.stem: A newly independent state in central Africa inherits borders drawn by a former colonial power, a handful of officials, no trained civil service, and a single export that pays the government's bills. Which step reduces the risk of collapse most?

options.text: Hand administration and customs to the strongest local authority that will accept a public accounting

options.misconception: assumes the inherited machinery is a benefit when there is no one trained to run it
options.text: Keep every official and every tariff the previous government used, since the machinery already works

options.misconception: sees the export income as the danger, when it is what funds the state at all
options.text: Close the borders to exports, since mineral shipments attract rival powers and outside claimants

options.misconception: concedes the revenue permanently, which is what a collapsing state can least afford
options.text: Give the export revenue to foreign buyers now, since stable income settles the political question

questions.explanation: The state has a map it did not choose, no officials, and one export, so what it lacks is an administration that can collect taxes and pay troops, and the fastest way to get one is to put the existing local hierarchy in charge under accounts it must show, because a government that cannot account cannot fund itself at all. The tempting answers keep a machinery nobody can run, shut off the only income, or hand that income away permanently, which is what a collapsing state can least afford.
questions.hint: What is the state shortest of, given the export it does have?

questions.topic: The canal crisis of 1956
questions.learningObjective: explain what the failed invasion settled about decolonization
questions.stem: A government in Cairo took over a foreign-owned canal company and closed the waterway to British ships, and Britain answered with an invasion that failed inside a week. Explain what the episode settled.

options.text: Force could not reverse a nationalization, so decolonization in the region became hard to undo

options.misconception: claims the invasion achieved its aims, when it was forced to withdraw within days
options.text: The canal was reopened on British terms, since the invasion achieved everything it had set out to do

options.misconception: invents an agreed division of traffic that the episode did not produce
options.text: The three empires agreed a share of the passage, so the dispute closed the question for all of them

options.misconception: explains the outcome by compensation, which is a way of buying a result not achieving it
options.text: The war ended because the owners were compensated, so the nationalization was allowed to stand

The tempting answers report a British success, invent an agreed division of traffic, and explain the outcome by compensation rather than by the failure that produced it.
questions.hint: Ask what a state's military reach is worth when the position is a few hundred miles away.

questions.topic: One state refuses to decolonize
questions.learningObjective: explain why decolonization was costly for one European economy
questions.stem: One European state refused to begin decolonization after 1945 and fought wars in two overseas territories until the mid-1970s. Why did decolonization cost that state so much?

options.text: The empire was large and rich, so the state had nothing to gain from granting political independence

options.misconception: calls the wars cheap and imported, though two of them ran for over a decade
options.text: The overseas wars were cheap, since the state fought only because its rivals demanded the land

options.misconception: puts the wars after recognition of independence, which is the reverse of the sequence
options.text: The colonies had already voted for independence, so the wars came after the state accepted the result

questions.explanation: A state whose industry runs on wages far below its own and on raw materials it does not produce cannot afford to lose the colonies, because independence would raise its labour costs and its import bill at the same moment as it lost the revenue, so the regime stayed until the wars and the empire could no longer be carried. The tempting answers call the empire rich, call the wars cheap, and put them after a recognition of independence that the sequence plainly precedes.
questions.hint: Ask what the home economy would lose besides the market: think about wages and raw materials.

questions.topic: Settlement in Algeria, 1962
questions.learningObjective: evaluate why the war in Algeria ended in negotiation
questions.stem: By 1962 the French government faced street violence in its own capital, a failed putsch by its own officers, and threats to leave the alliance, and then opened talks that ended the war in Algeria within months. What made a settlement possible then?

options.text: Authority at home was collapsing, so continuing the war would have cost the regime more than conceding did

options.misconception: claims a decisive military success by French forces that had been losing the war
options.text: The army had won every engagement, so a negotiated settlement was the only way left to stop the fighting

options.misconception: confuses a negotiated transfer of authority with a change in where the fighting took place
options.text: The border was indefensible, so the government chose to move the fighting outside the country

options.misconception: assumes an external deadline, where the pressure came from inside the country
options.text: The other powers set a deadline, so Paris had no choice but to sign whatever was put on the table

The tempting answers claim an unbroken military record, invent a defensive border, and attribute the reversal to a foreign deadline when the pressure was internal.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the war was actually deciding the outcome by 1962.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two accounts of the 1950s economic boom
questions.learningObjective: synthesize two explanations of the postwar recovery
questions.stem: Two original summaries of the 1950s explain rising output and living standards differently: one credits cheap imported energy and new American equipment, the other credits markets opened when colonial empires stopped competing with home producers. Which synthesis fits both?

options.text: Both point to low input costs and new export sales, which together explain the rising output and wages

options.misconception: collapses two distinct causes into one, which is what a synthesis must avoid
options.text: Both agree on a single cause, since cheap energy alone produced the same result in every country

options.misconception: treats the second summary as contributing nothing, though it names a real change
options.text: One summary names a cause and the other names nothing, so they cannot be combined at all

options.misconception: reads cheap imports as fatal to home industry rather than as a cost advantage
options.text: The two are opposites, since cheap imports destroyed the factories that made the high wages possible

questions.explanation: Cheap inputs and newly available export sales are not rival explanations but two halves of the same account: lower costs let firms expand, and more markets let them sell, so output and real wages rise together and the reconstruction demand that started the process is what both summaries share. The tempting answers force a single cause, declare one summary empty, or read cheap imports as the destruction of the industry rather than as the reason it could compete.
questions.hint: Ask whether a low cost of production and a new market for goods can both be true at once.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The clearing union that broke down
questions.learningObjective: recall why a common payments fund could not hold
questions.stem: The European recovery programme was followed in 1950 by a clearing union in which member states settled trade balances through a common fund instead of bilateral debts. Why did the arrangement break down within a few years?

options.text: Trade balances were never equal, so credits piled up in one state and the fund could not be drained

options.misconception: denies the cross-border trade the whole arrangement was built to settle
options.text: Member states kept their borders closed, so there was no cross-border trade for it to clear

options.misconception: invents a gold dispute that the fund's own rules made impossible to raise late on
options.text: The fund's gold was drained by its members, so the accounts were closed before first payment fell due

options.misconception: confuses a clearing system with a currency union it never created
options.text: The union replaced national currencies at once, so governments lost the right to set their own rates

questions.explanation: A common fund works only while members owe one another roughly the same amount, and one state with a persistent surplus keeps drawing on the fund until it is empty, so the arrangement broke on the imbalance it was designed to absorb rather than on any dispute about its rules. The tempting answers say there was no trade to clear, invent a gold run the accounts do not show, and confuse a clearing system with a common currency it never created.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a shared pot when one member earns a large and lasting surplus.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Heavy investment and scarce consumer goods
questions.learningObjective: explain the priorities behind the eastern bloc economy
questions.stem: Shop goods stayed scarce across the eastern bloc through the 1950s while steel output, new plants, and heavy investment rose every year. Which explanation best fits that pattern?

options.text: Decisions and resources went to heavy industry and the space effort, so consumer lines were crowded out

options.misconception: assumes a market economy, which is the opposite of how the bloc allocated resources
options.text: The bloc followed the market, so scarce goods reflected too few shops rather than a policy choice

options.misconception: blames distribution for output the investment figures show was never produced
options.text: Consumer factories ran well, so the reported scarcity came from a failure of distribution in the towns

options.misconception: denies the arms and space spending that the heavy investment figures largely record
options.text: Arms production was small, so the heavy investment must have gone to consumer goods that never arrived

questions.explanation: A command economy that sets every price by decision can put workers and steel wherever the leadership decides, so a standing priority on heavy industry and the space effort consumes the inputs that consumer lines would need, and scarce shelves are the predictable result of that choice rather than a failure of distribution. The tempting answers assume prices were set by buyers, blame shops for goods that were never made, and deny the arms and space spending the investment figures mostly record.
questions.hint: Ask who decides what the steel goes into when the state owns the works.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reformers who exposed the gap between promise and practice
questions.learningObjective: explain why a reform movement was removed so quickly
questions.stem: Reformers in one eastern state in 1956 won support by publishing how far practice had departed from the system's own stated promises, and their first act was to remove a long-time leader. Why did the change end so quickly?

options.text: Publishing the gap threatened the legitimacy of every state in the bloc, so it was stopped at once

options.misconception: denies the popular support the reformers' public campaign plainly won
options.text: The reformers had no support in the cities, so the change failed because the crowds turned against them

options.misconception: credits the state with no armed force, which the intervention itself disproves
options.text: The state had no armed forces of its own, so the reformers could hold the capital for a week

options.misconception: reduces a foreign intervention to an internal vote that the same party controlled
options.text: The party's own members voted the change back, so no outside force was involved at all

questions.explanation: A bloc survives by every member's claim to legitimacy, and a state that publishes the distance between its laws and its practice is not making a local complaint but handing every other government the same document, so the bloc leader had to remove the reformers to stop the example rather than to settle a dispute inside one country. The tempting answers deny the crowds, invent a government without an army, and reduce a foreign intervention to an internal vote.
questions.hint: Ask what a published list of broken promises does to the other members of the group.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Invasion and the limits of a written promise
questions.learningObjective: analyze what an intervention proved about the system's own rules
questions.stem: Reformers in 1968 wrote new rights into a state that had already signed them, expecting the earlier promise to be honoured, and the response was invasion. Why did the episode settle what the earlier promise was worth?

options.text: The written rights proved unenforceable, so any future reform had to expect removal by force instead

options.misconception: reads a demonstrated failure of enforcement as a demonstration that promises hold
options.text: The invasion proved the written promise was binding, so the reformers had found the legal way forward

options.misconception: makes the episode a moral verdict on ideas rather than a test of enforcement
options.text: The invasion showed the reformers had chosen the wrong ideas, so the retreat was a moral defeat only

options.misconception: explains a political intervention with a shortage the episode never mentions
options.text: The invasion showed the state was poor, so the government changed its policy from want of money

questions.explanation: A right written into law is only worth what the state will enforce against itself, and an invasion sent to stop reformers who had merely cited that law is the clearest possible demonstration that the law does not bind the government that signed it, which is why later reformers no longer trusted promises and the system settled into a long period of no change at all. The tempting answers read the failure of enforcement as proof that promises bind, treat it as a moral verdict, and invent a financial cause.
questions.hint: Ask what an invasion proves about the value of a right the government itself granted.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Closing the sector boundary in Berlin
questions.learningObjective: recall what the barrier was built to stop
questions.stem: In August 1961 the eastern authorities began sealing the boundary between the sectors of one city with wire, then a wall, and armed guards, and the western side never tried to force it open. What was the boundary meant to secure?

options.text: A steady outward flight of skilled workers, so the state first sealed the border and then built a wall

options.misconception: credits the eastern state with granting the free movement the barrier in fact ended
options.text: The right of the western allies to move freely, so the barrier settled a dispute about visits

options.misconception: presents the barrier as insurance against a foreign claim on the whole city
options.text: The claim of another power to the whole city, so the wall guarded against a western takeover

options.misconception: misreads a barrier against movement as a measure about the two currency areas
options.text: The currency of the eastern zone, so the wall kept the new banknotes from being spent in the west

questions.explanation: A state whose young and skilled leave through an open boundary loses the people its economy and its army are built on, and a barrier stops that flow at the moment the state's own construction and hiring depend on it, so the wall is a labour and conscription measure as much as a border. The tempting answers credit the barrier with granting free movement, invent a foreign claim on the city, and read it as a currency measure rather than a measure about people.
questions.hint: Ask who was crossing the boundary in one direction while the building went up.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A nuclear standoff settled by a secret European concession
questions.learningObjective: interpret a crisis summary for the European bargain inside it
questions.stem: An original summary of a 1962 exchange records that one side had placed missiles in Cuba, the other had missiles in a European country, and that both quietly withdrew them within a fortnight while announcing nothing to their allies. What does the exchange establish?

options.text: Each side removed a threat the other could not show, so the settlement rested on a kept secret

options.misconception: reduces a missile standoff to a naval action, which the summary never mentions
options.text: The exchange shows a sea battle decided the matter, since missiles had no reach in the Caribbean

options.misconception: denies the mutual pressure the summary's paired withdrawals make explicit
options.text: The exchange proves the quarrel was local, since neither side pressed the other anywhere at all

options.misconception: claims a shooting war the withdrawals instead prevented
options.text: The exchange shows the crisis ended in war, since both sides fired before withdrawing anything

questions.explanation: Two sets of missiles removed, no announcement, and no protest from the ally left out of the bargain: that is the signature of a trade in which each side removes what the other cannot prove it still holds, and it is why the crisis ended without a public settlement and why the two governments afterwards built the direct line and the test ban that reduce the chance of the next one. The tempting answers substitute a sea battle, deny the mutual pressure, and claim a war the withdrawals prevented.
questions.hint: Ask why neither government told the ally whose missiles were the price of the deal.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Prices, production, and jobs after the oil shock
questions.learningObjective: read a price-output series as a supply shock
questions.stem: A table for 1973 to 1975 shows the price of imported oil rising several times over, consumer prices following a year later, and output and employment falling together. What best explains that sequence?

options.text: A costlier imported input fed into consumer prices and then squeezed output and jobs, as a supply shock does

options.misconception: reads a cost shock as a demand boom, which would raise output rather than lower it
options.text: A costlier imported input raised demand for goods, which is the pattern a boom in output produces

options.misconception: reverses the direction of causation between the oil price and shop prices
options.text: Shop prices rose first and pulled the oil price after them, since inflation usually begins in the shops

options.misconception: inverts the price change the table records in every one of the three columns
options.text: Output and jobs fell because the oil price fell, since cheaper fuel can only shrink an economy

questions.explanation: Oil is an input that every industrial economy buys from outside, so when its price multiplies, firms that cannot pass the cost on cut output and employment, and consumer prices follow with a lag as the cost moves through the chain, which is the sequence the table prints. The tempting answers turn a cost shock into a demand boom, reverse the order of cause and effect between oil and shop prices, and claim a fall in the oil price that the same table denies.
questions.hint: Follow the order of the columns: which price moves first, and what happens next.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Opening talks with the eastern government
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the domestic cost of a policy of accommodation
questions.stem: A West German chancellor in the early 1970s opened negotiations with the eastern government, accepted that the border dividing Germany would stand, and hoped that trade and contact would change the other side. Why was this hard to defend at home?

options.text: Accepting the border conceded the division he had promised to undo, so his own party called it betrayal

options.misconception: assumes total refusal, which the opening of negotiations and its results contradict
options.text: The eastern government refused all contact, so the policy produced no result of any kind at all

options.misconception: denies the commercial argument the policy deliberately relied upon
options.text: Trade with the east raised eastern living standards, so the plan had no economic argument behind it

options.misconception: makes the partners the source of the difficulty, where the cost was paid at home
options.text: The western partners forbade any negotiation, so the chancellor defended a policy they rejected

questions.explanation: A leader who has promised that the division will not stand cannot concede the division in order to improve it, and the concession is visible at once while the hoped-for change is invisible and may never come, so he is judged on the visible half of the bargain alone. The tempting answers claim no contact was possible, deny the commercial motive, and blame the western partners when the political cost fell on his own side.
questions.hint: Ask which half of the bargain the voters can see.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A government overthrown by its own officers
questions.learningObjective: explain why an authoritarian regime fell from within
questions.stem: In 1974 officers in the middle ranks of one European state's armed forces overthrew a government that had ruled for four decades, and the country joined the European economic community a few years later. Why did the officers move?

options.text: The colonial wars had made the government's programme impossible to pay for, so field officers struck first

options.misconception: invents an outside takeover, which is the opposite of how the change happened
options.text: A foreign invasion ended the fighting, so the officers were rewarded by the government they replaced

options.misconception: calls the economy recovered, when exhaustion and the war are what the officers objected to
options.text: The economy had already recovered, so the officers acted to stop any further reform of wages

options.misconception: puts the monarchy behind a coup that its own position could not survive
options.text: The monarchy ordered the change, so the officers were acting on instructions from the crown

questions.explanation: A government that has spent four decades on wars it cannot finance and cannot end is spending the obedience of the very officers who have to carry them out, and when an order becomes impossible to carry the men closest to the job decide what to do next, which is why the change came from the middle ranks and not from the opposition. The tempting answers invent a foreign invasion, claim an economy that had already recovered, and put the crown behind a coup that would have destroyed the crown.
questions.hint: Ask which men carried out the policy and what it was costing them personally.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two accounts of the last decade of one eastern state
questions.learningObjective: synthesize internal and external causes of a regime's collapse
questions.stem: Two original summaries of one country's last decade disagree: one traces the change to unions and strikes that forced a government to negotiate, the other to a neighbouring collapse and a sponsor's decision not to intervene. Which synthesis fits both?

options.text: Pressure inside and retreat outside combined, since the government conceded reform as the sponsor withdrew

options.misconception: makes the internal pressure sufficient by itself, which the summary's external half denies
options.text: Internal pressure explains the whole change, since the unions alone forced every concession

options.misconception: makes the external retreat sufficient by itself, which the summary's internal half denies
options.text: External retreat explains the whole change, since the neighbouring collapse did what the unions did not

options.misconception: dismisses both summaries for an unnamed event, which is not a synthesis of anything
options.text: Neither summary is useful, since the change came from a single event both accounts leave out

questions.explanation: The two summaries describe a sequence rather than a contradiction: a government that cannot reform has to concede when its own workers stop working, but conceding is only safe when the state that has been propping it up declines to step in, so the external retreat is what makes the internal pressure safe to yield to. The tempting answers make either half sufficient on its own, which is exactly the reading the other summary rules out, and the last one dismisses both without explaining anything.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two halves had to come first for the other to work.
